system.name: centroid-based deanonymization of text-to-image leaderboards
system.one_liner: An attack that identifies which text-to-image model made an image by matching its embedding to model-specific clusters, breaking leaderboard anonymity.

content.variant_note: a voting arena, a prompt database, candidate models and a hooded adversary exchanging prompts, votes and rankings, with the attacker's embedding pipeline inside a red dashed frame
content.argues: Images of each T2I model form separate clusters in embedding space, so an adversary can identify the model behind anonymous leaderboard images and then steer votes.
content.subject: A voting leaderboard shows a prompt and two anonymous images; an adversary embeds them, matches model clusters and submits votes that change the ranking.

lessons.what_to_learn: Draw a threat model by putting the adversary icon on the border of a dashed frame that holds its pipeline, tie its actions to the victim system with dotted arrows, and end on the consequence (changed rankings on a podium). Show the key mechanism as a plain scatter whose colours match the sample stacks that produced it.
lessons.suits: Threat-model, privacy or attack papers where an adversary acts on a platform and a representation-space mechanism (clusters, fingerprints) makes the attack work.

evidence: In voting-based T2I leaderboards, users are provided a pair of image generations without any information about the underlying generation model
Overview of our setting: (a) voting-based leaderboard and (b) adversarial deanonymization pipeline leveraging model-specific clustering in embedding space.

summary: The paper shows that anonymity in voting-based text-to-image leaderboards can be broken: each model's images form their own cluster in an image-embedding space, so an adversary can tell which model made an image without controlling prompts. Figure 1 draws the setting in one picture. On the left, a voting arena shows a prompt and two anonymous generations from two of the listed models, and a hooded adversary icon watches. Inside a red dashed frame at the right, the adversary embeds the two images, matches them to colour-coded clusters built from image stacks of the candidate models, and then submits votes that change the model rankings on a trophy podium.

notes: Prior labels kept. The caption names panels (a) and (b), but the printed figure carries no letters: (b) is the red dashed frame, (a) the unframed left part, so both panel labels are null. The dotted versus solid arrow meaning is my reading and is not keyed in the figure. Icon counts follow what is visible (the digest lists 33 placed bitmaps). The embedding model is drawn as a network glyph; the T2I models are drawn as logos.
